unclear. In this analysis, we considered diet as the exposure and sleep characteristics as potential
mediators between diet and microbiome species abundance. We have revised the sentence in the
Discussion to: “When considering diet as the exposure and sleep characteristics as potential mediators,
we identified some connections that suggest a direct link between sleep patterns and variations in species
abundance.”
Reviewer #2:
The manuscript presents a comprehensive analysis of the bidirectional relationship between sleep
characteristics and gut microbiome composition in a large-scale Dutch cohort. The integration of various
statistical methods, metagenomic sequencing that ensures detailed taxonomic profiling at the species
level, improving our understanding of the complex interplay between sleep and gut microbiome
composition. The identification of specific bacterial species associated with distinct sleep parameters is
particularly interesting. However, some areas, such as the analysis methods and interpretation of results,
require further clarification and additional analysis to strengthen the conclusions. Our specific comments
are:
Point 1: Lines 241-243: The authors report a “consistent directional trend” across species associated with
positive sleep characteristics. This interpretation as a biologically meaningful finding is questionable.
Instead, the trend could be due to the use of measurement tools that assess overlapping components of
sleep, which would result in a technical artifact rather than a genuine biological phenomenon. This
alternative explanation warrants explicit consideration in the manuscript.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable point. Indeed, the consistent directional trend we
observed across species may be partly due to correlations among the sleep measures. To address this,
we have now explicitly pointed it out and revised the corresponding part of the Results section: “Among
the 137 species identified, we observed a consistent directional trend, whereby a species associated with
a positive sleep characteristic (e.g., good sleep quality) tended to also associate positively with other
favorable sleep characteristics (e.g., reduced social jet lag). This may suggest a shared biological basis
underlying different aspects of sleep, although some of the observed consistency could also reflect
overlap among the sleep measures.”
characteristics raises concerns about its biological significance. This finding could be influenced by
differences in data distributions across the sleep measurements. For instance, as shown in Figure 1b,
most sleep quality measures are concentrated at the good-quality end with decent variability, while social
jet lag measurements show limited variability at the good-quality end and are skewed towards poor
quality. Furthermore, the analyses for social jet lag and chronotype may lack sufficient statistical power,
making the results potentially driven by random noise. In contrast, the analysis for sleep quality appears
better powered. This discrepancy makes the comparability of significant features across the three sleep
characteristics questionable and requires further discussion.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful comment. While we agree that the original
distributions of sleep traits differ (Figure 1b), we note that in the association analyses, sleep quality (PSQI)
and social jet lag were treated as continuous variables and normalized using inverse rank transformation.
This approach minimizes the impact of non-normal distributions and helps maintain comparable
statistical power across these traits. Chronotype, on the other hand, was categorized into three ordinal
groups (early, intermediate, late), coded as 0, 1, and 2. We acknowledge that the limited number of
categories for chronotype could introduce some granularity and potentially reduce power compared to
fully continuous traits. We have clarified this point in the Results section while keeping the main text
concise to maintain readability: “Most of the sleep–species associations we identified were uniquely
linked to a specific sleep aspect: 101 species were exclusively associated with sleep quality, 8 with social
jet lag, and 7 with chronotype. The larger number of associations we observed for sleep quality might not
only indicate stronger biological connections, it could also partly result from greater variability in the sleep
quality data compared to other sleep measures.”
Point 3: In this study, the authors described that alpha diversity was inversely associated with sleep
quality. This is somehow an inaccurate description, and it needs to be rephrased. According to the results,
alpha diversity was inversely associated with PSQI score in this study, not sleep quality, as a higher score
implies lower sleep quality. Nevertheless, this result is consistent with the notion that a higher microbiome
diversity is generally more positively related to health.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important suggestion. To improve precision, we have revised the
wording in both the Abstract and the Results section. In the Abstract, we now state: “We found that lower
alpha diversity was associated with poorer sleep quality, later chronotype, and greater social jet lag.” In
the Results section, we specify: “Alpha diversity, as measured by the Shannon index, was significantly
associated with PSQI score (Beta = -0.015, P-value = 0.017),” thereby clearly indicating that the
association was with the PSQI score, where higher values reflect poorer sleep quality.
Point 4: Mediation analysis: The authors' approach to mediation analysis is conceptually flawed. Proper
causal mediation analysis requires a pre-specified directed acyclic graph (DAG) and adherence to critical
assumptions, including correct model specification. The practice of rotating the roles of exposure,
mediator, and outcome to fit different causal mediation models based on statistical significance is
fundamentally incorrect. A model should be defined a priori and not selected post hoc based on results.
The authors are strongly encouraged to read through VanderWeele's Explanation in Causal Inference:
Methods for Mediation and Interaction (2015) for proper methodology. Additionally, the study may violate
two key assumptions of causal mediation analysis: (1) temporality, i.e., the exposure, mediator, and
outcome are measured sequentially; and (2) no unmeasured confounding, as the adjustment for
10
confounders is likely to be insufficient. Finally, addressing high dimensionality upfront in the modeling
process, rather than adopting a two-step approach, is critical to avoid overfitting and false positives.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s careful critique and fully agree that causal mediation analysis
requires strong assumptions, including a clearly specified causal structure, temporally ordered variables,
and appropriate adjustment for confounding. We would like to clarify that our study employs mediation
analysis in an exploratory, hypothesis-generating context, rather than to make formal causal claims.
To avoid post hoc model selection, all directional models were pre-specified based on biological
plausibility. Specifically, we defined three directional hypotheses involving diet (diet → microbiome →
sleep, diet → sleep → microbiome, sleep → diet → microbiome) and two involving disease (disease →
microbiome → sleep, sleep → microbiome → disease). The diet models were selected based on the
recognition that diet is generally considered upstream of the microbiome due to its well-established role
as a primary modulator of microbial composition. For the disease-related models, we explored these
directions to assess the potential for the gut microbiome to act as a mediator. If such mediation exists, it
could point toward microbiome-targeted strategies for disease prevention or intervention. These five
directions were tested consistently across all combinations, independent of statistical significance. We
did not rotate the roles of exposure, mediator, and outcome based on results. This structure was
established prior to analysis to ensure clarity and interpretability.
We acknowledge that our cross-sectional design limits our ability to establish temporality and that
unmeasured confounding remains a possibility despite extensive covariate adjustment. We have now
made these limitations more explicit in the revised manuscript and have taken care to frame our findings
as exploratory and hypothesis-generating. We hope our results will inform future studies that can more
directly assess causal relationships using longitudinal or interventional designs.
With respect to high dimensionality, we recognize the importance of minimizing overfitting and controlling
false positives. In our approach, the univariable mediation analysis served as a screening step to reduce
the dimensionality of microbial features prior to multivariable modeling. Including all ~200 microbial
variables in a single penalized model can result in excessive shrinkage and unreliable effect estimation,
making pre-selection a necessary compromise. The final effect estimates were obtained solely from the
penalized multivariable model, which applies an L1 (lasso) penalty to enable robust variable selection and
effect estimation. We believe this strategy improves model stability and interpretability while helping to
mitigate the risk of overfitting in a high-dimensional setting.
We have revised the manuscript accordingly to clarify the exploratory nature of our mediation analysis, the
assumptions involved, and the rationale behind our modeling strategy. These revisions are now reflected
in:
Method: “A large proportion of the associations we observed between sleep characteristics and other
traits were related to dietary patterns, GI discomfort, and mental health conditions. Given that diet is a
well-established modulator of the gut microbiome, and GI and mental disorders often co-occur with both
sleep disturbances and microbiome alterations, we sought to explore the potential causal relationships
between sleep, the microbiome, and either diet or disease. Based on biological plausibility, we pre-
specified a set of hypothesized models for mediation analysis. For diet, we tested three plausible pathways:
(i) diet → microbiome → sleep, (ii) diet → sleep → microbiome, and (iii) sleep → diet → microbiome. For
disease-related traits (GI symptoms and mental health disorders), we tested models where the
microbiome may mediate the relationship between disease and sleep: (i) disease → microbiome → sleep
and (ii) sleep → microbiome → disease.
Across all models, microbial variables included two types of features: (i) relative abundances of 137
microbial species previously found to be associated with at least one sleep phenotype and (ii) measures
11
of overall microbiome composition. For alpha diversity, we included Shannon index and PD. For beta
diversity, we computed the first 20 principal coordinates (PCoAs) based on weighted UniFrac distances.
For sleep characteristics, we focused on variables that demonstrated a significant link with species
abundance, namely sleep quality, social jet lag, and chronotype. Dietary variables included the Healthy
Eating Index (HEI), protein score, alcohol consumption (adjusted for total caloric intake), alternative
Mediterranean diet score (aMED), modified Mediterranean diet score (mMED), plant protein score, coffee
consumption, total caloric intake, low carbohydrate score, and free sugar intake. The GI phenotypes
included celiac disease, Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis, stomach ulcer, and general GI discomfort
including abdominal pain, bloating, flatulence, burping, and nausea. The mental health phenotypes
included bipolar disorder, depression, eating disorder, generalized anxiety, and panic disorder. All
microbial variables were adjusted for technical factors (sequencing batch, DNA concentration, and post-
QC read count), stool characteristics (Bristol Stool Scale, defecation frequency), and intrinsic factors (age
and sex). All other variables were also adjusted for age and sex. Residuals from these adjusted models
were used as inputs to the mediation framework to reduce confounding by known covariates.
As an initial screening step, we conducted univariable mediation analyses using the mediate function from
the mediation R package39, systematically testing all relevant combinations of exposures, mediators, and
outcomes across the pre-specified model directions (Table S8–9). This function estimates the average
causal mediation effect and average direct effect based on two linear models: a mediator model
(regressing the mediator on the exposure) and an outcome model (regressing the outcome on both the
exposure and mediator). For each exposure–mediator–outcome triplet, the mediation effect and its
significance were estimated using quasi-Bayesian Monte Carlo simulation with 1,000 draws. These
univariable models served as an exploratory filter to identify candidate variables for multivariable analysis.
Triplets with a mediation P-value < 0.05 were considered nominally significant, and microbiome variables
that appeared in at least one significant triplet were retained for further modeling using a regularized
multivariable mediation framework.
Next, multivariable mediation effects for each direction were estimated using selected microbiome
variables using the regmed package in R for regularized mediation analysis via penalized structural
equation modeling40. Variable selection in the regularized mediation model was performed using a lasso-
penalized model, with the optimal lambda for the lasso (L1) penalty determined by minimizing the
Bayesian Information Criterion through a grid search41. A non-penalized model incorporating the identified
variables was then employed to compute precise effect sizes. For each pathway, the proportion of
mediation attributable to the mediator was quantified based on the effect sizes from the non-penalized
model. This proportion was determined by dividing the mediated effect (the product of the pathways from
X to the mediator and from the mediator to Y) by the total effect (the sum of the mediated effect and any
direct effect).”
Results: “Having established a link between sleep and bacterial composition, we sought to determine
whether alterations in sleep patterns influence microbial species abundance and diversity measures, or if
the reverse is true. To investigate this, we incorporated dietary patterns, which we hypothesized to be more
likely to be an exposure than a consequence of the microbial features, into our mediation network analysis.
This analysis tested three predefined potential directional relationships: (i) diet → microbiome → sleep,
where changes in microbial features potentially cause alterations in sleep characteristics, (ii) diet → sleep
→ microbiome, and (iii) sleep → diet → microbiome, where changes in microbial features are outcomes of
lifestyle modifications.
In the first scenario (Figure 4a, Table S10), we observed that most species demonstrated a direct link to
either sleep or diet. However, two species, Clostridia bacterium UC5_1_1E11 and Clostridia unclassified
SGB14844 (both from the unclassified Clostridia genus), acted as putative mediators in the diet-to-sleep
12
pathway, suggesting a potential mediation of the effect of coffee consumption on social jet lag. Increased
coffee intake was found to boost the abundance of these two species, consequently intensifying the extent
of social jet lag. This interesting dynamic between coffee consumption, the two Clostridia species, and
social jet lag was also observed in the second (Figure 4b, Table S11) and third scenarios (Figure 4c, Table
S12), indicating that fluctuations in social jet lag might impact coffee consumption, or vice versa, thereby
altering the abundance of these two Clostridia species.
Since these two species appeared in a mediation relationship in all three directions, we could quantify the
proportion of mediation based on effect sizes derived from an unpenalized model (Figure 4d). By
aggregating the effects of UC5_1_1E11 and SGB14844, we discovered that the abundance of these species
mediated 10% of the effect of coffee intake on social jet lag. Conversely, social jet lag accounted for only
1.7% of the effect of coffee intake on these species. Notably, coffee intake was found to mediate 59.8% of
the effect of social jet lag on these species. These estimates suggest that variation in the abundance of
these two Clostridia species related to social jet lag may largely reflect differences in coffee consumption.
To further investigate the functional and evolutionary basis of these two Clostridia species, we conducted
exploratory analyses of their metabolic pathways and phylogenetic relationships. Despite their putative
role in mediation, we identified no significant (FDR < 0.05) metabolic pathways or phylogenetic
conservation of these species’ associations with social jet lag or coffee intake (Table S13–14). While their
functional roles remain unclear, these species could influence circadian rhythms through unmeasured
metabolites or indirect mechanisms, warranting deeper functional profiling in targeted studies.
Along the same line, the connections between many microbial features and sleep characteristics were
found to be potentially mediated by specific dietary factors (direction III) (Figure 4c, Table S12). Similar to
the two Clostridia species, many species abundances could also be affected by changes in coffee
consumption induced by social jet lag. Lachnospiraceae GGB3570_SGB4777, Ruminococcaceae
GGB9623_SGB15076, and Clostridium phoceensis showed an increase following coffee intake, while
Ruminococcaceae GGB9699_SGB15216 exhibited a decrease. Additionally, a preference for a later
chronotype was linked with increased alcohol consumption, which in turn led to a reduced abundance of
Coprococcus eutactus. Poor sleep quality associated with a lower HEI led to an increased abundance of
Flavonifractor plautii. Nevertheless, findings from direction II still revealed that certain species do exhibit
a direct connection with sleep patterns, independent of dietary mediation (Figure 4b, Table S11). For
example, individuals with a late chronotype displayed elevated levels of Lachnospiraceae
GGB3570_SGB4777 and a reduction in Clostridium sp. Marseille P3244 and Clostridium leptum.
To extend the analysis beyond dietary exposures, we also evaluated whether the gut microbiome could
serve as a mediator in associations between sleep characteristics and disease phenotypes, focusing on
GI symptoms and mental health conditions (Table S15-16). However, we did not identify any microbial
features or diversity measures that met the criteria for significant mediation in these models.”
Discussion: “Another compelling area for future research involves uncovering the true causal links
between sleep-related disorders, sleep patterns, and the gut microbiome through intervention or
experimental studies. However, this topic was beyond the scope of our current study. Given the cross-
sectional nature of our data, establishing definitive directionality is challenging because any of the factors
could be hypothesized as exposures, mediators, or outcomes, resulting in six different hypothetical
scenarios for analysis. While dealing with such complexity using cross-sectional data is challenging,
exploring these aspects through future longitudinal studies could help deepen our understanding of these
complex relationships.
As mentioned, one of the major limitations of our study is its cross-sectional design, which prevents us
from establishing the temporal order of events. This is particularly relevant for mediation analysis, where
13
a clear sequence of exposure, mediator, and outcome is required to support causal interpretation. In
addition, although we adjusted for a broad set of known covariates, we cannot exclude the possibility of
unmeasured confounding. Therefore, the mediation results should be viewed as exploratory and
interpreted with caution. Moreover, the reliance on self-reported data for both sleep patterns and dietary
habits introduces potential reporting bias. Although self-reporting is valuable for gathering data in large-
scale studies, it is prone to inaccuracies and personal biases. Objective measurements, such as
actigraphy for sleep and detailed diet logs or biomarkers for dietary intake, would enhance the validity of
results.”
Point 5: The study highlights the role of dietary factors in mediating microbiome changes, but direct effects
of diet on sleep characteristics is not discussed in this study. Could you explore more direct relationships
between specific dietary patterns (e.g., Mediterranean diet) and sleep quality or chronotype independent
of microbiome mediation? At least you should provide it in the discussion.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the helpful suggestion. Associations of sleep characteristics and
dietary patterns are presented in Figure 2. In the result section we wrote: “Our results showed that
individuals with optimal health status exhibited more favorable sleep characteristics. Conversely,
suboptimal sleep—defined by lower sleep quality, increased daytime sleepiness, greater social jet lag,
and a tendency toward a late chronotype—was linked to a spectrum of health issues, notably psychological
and GI disorders. Regarding dietary habits, a healthy diet, as indicated by high HEI scores and increased
intake of polysaccharides and proteins, was associated with better sleep metrics. In contrast, diets
characterized by adherence to a Western pattern and higher intake of maltose were associated with poorer
sleep parameters. Notably, alcohol consumption was linked to a later chronotype (P-value = 1.38×10-40),
whereas higher total caloric intake was related to increased daytime sleepiness (P-value = 4.47×10-25).”
We have now also added a paragraph to the Discussion to highlight the strong link between diet and sleep
observed in our current analyses. The added text reads: “By incorporating dietary factors, we were able to
conduct a comprehensive mediation analysis. Diet showed strong direct associations with sleep
characteristics; for example, a higher Healthy Eating Index (HEI) was directly linked to better sleep quality,
earlier chronotype, and reduced social jet lag; coffee and alcohol consumption were linked to chronotype
and social jet lag; and higher alternative Mediterranean diet scores (aMED) and low-carbohydrate diet
scores were linked to chronotype. All these associations were observed in both directions.”
Point 6: The results presented in Figure 3 lack clarity regarding whether they are multivariable-adjusted.
If the models described in the methods were used, additional confounders such as physical activity,
sedentary time, dietary quality, total energy intake, alcohol consumption, hypertension,
hypercholesterolemia, diabetes, and relevant medications (e.g., sleep aids, melatonin)
should also be included. Given the observational nature of the study, adjusting for these variables is essential to
strengthen the robustness of the conclusions.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for underscoring the importance of robust confounding control. In the revised
manuscript, we have updated Figure 3 caption to explicitly indicate that the results are based on
multivariable-adjusted models, accounting for age, sex, BMI, batch, DNA concentration, Bristol Stool
Scale, and defecation frequency.
We have also conducted supplementary analyses adjusting for the additional confounders suggested.
Specifically, we included physical activity, alcohol consumption, metabolic diseases (hypertension,
hypercholesterolemia, and diabetes), alcohol consumption, dietary quality (Healthy Eating Index [HEI]),
total energy intake, and use of sleep-aid medications, in addition to GI symptoms and mental diseases.
The results of these extended adjustments are presented in the updated Supplementary Figure S6.
Adjusting for each covariate individually did not substantially alter the observed associations, indicating
that our findings are robust to these potential confounders. Adjustment for sleep-aid medication slightly
changed the association with PSQI scores. This is likely because the global PSQI score already
incorporates information on sleep medication use (specifically through component 6), and thus adjusting
for medication use separately could introduce overadjustment. In addition, we examined a fully adjusted
model incorporating all covariates simultaneously. Although the strength of some associations was
slightly attenuated due to a reduction in sample size from missing data, the overall directionality and
consistency of the findings were preserved. These results further support the robustness of our
conclusions. We have updated the Methods and Results sections and Supplementary Figure S6 to
document these analyses.
Method: “To account for the potential confounding effects of various factors on the gut microbiome, we
included the following factors as covariates when conducting any analyses related to the microbial
features: technical parameters (metagenomic sequencing batch number, DNA concentration (ng/µl), and
number of post-quality control reads), intrinsic factors (age, sex, and BMI), and stool characteristics
(frequency and consistency measured by Bristol Stool Scale).
To assess the robustness of species abundance associations with sleep characteristics, we performed a
series of sensitivity analyses, adjusting individually for additional potential confounders, including
metabolic diseases (hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and diabetes), GI diseases, mental health
conditions, physical activity, alcohol intake, and sleep medication use. We also examined a fully adjusted
model incorporating all covariates simultaneously.”
Result: “In our previous analysis, we had observed strong links between sleep characteristics and mental
or GI diseases. To assess whether these or other health and lifestyle factors conditions were confounding
our results, we conducted a sensitivity analysis incorporating additional covariates, including mental
disease status, GI disease status, metabolic diseases (hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, diabetes),
physical activity, alcohol intake, and use of sleep medications in our model (Figure S6). The consistent
distribution of significance and direction of effect, even after accounting for these covariates individually
and jointly, indicates that the associations between sleep characteristics and microbial species are robust
and not driven by these potential confounders.”
Point 7: How do you reconcile the bidirectional relationship between sleep and the microbiome with the
observational nature of the data? Could longitudinal or interventional studies strengthen this aspect?
This needs to be at least addressed in the limitation section.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for the helpful comment. We have emphasized the limitations of our cross-
sectional design in the Discussion section: “Another compelling area for future research involves
uncovering the true causal links between sleep-related disorders, sleep patterns, and the gut microbiome
through intervention or experimental studies. However, this topic was beyond the scope of our current
study. Given the cross-sectional nature of our data, establishing definitive directionality is challenging
because any of the factors could be hypothesized as exposures, mediators, or outcomes, resulting in six
different hypothetical scenarios for analysis. While dealing with such complexity using cross-sectional
data is challenging, exploring these aspects through future longitudinal studies could help deepen our
understanding of these complex relationships.
As mentioned, one of the major limitations of our study is its cross-sectional design, which prevents us
from establishing the temporal order of events. This is particularly relevant for mediation analysis, where
15
a clear sequence of exposure, mediator, and outcome is required to support causal interpretation. In
addition, although we adjusted for a broad set of known covariates, we cannot exclude the possibility of
unmeasured confounding. Therefore, the mediation results should be viewed as exploratory and
interpreted with caution. Moreover, the reliance on self-reported data for both sleep patterns and dietary
habits introduces potential reporting bias. Although self-reporting is valuable for gathering data in large-
scale studies, it is prone to inaccuracies and personal biases. Objective measurements, such as
actigraphy for sleep and detailed diet logs or biomarkers for dietary intake, would enhance the validity of
results.”
Point 8: The analysis highlights the role of coffee consumption in modulating social jet lag through specific
species. There is a paper recently published (doi.org/10.1038/s41564-024-01858-9), showing the strong
link between coffee consumption and the species Lawsonibacter asaccharolyticus. How is the role of this
species in your data? Did it also show a relationship with coffee intake and sleep quality?
Response: Thank you for bringing this interesting recent finding to our attention. Indeed, we observe a
strong association between this particular species and both coffee intake and chronotype in our data.
However, in our study, this species is annotated as Clostridium phoceensis rather than Lawsonibacter
asaccharolyticus. As noted in the original study, “However, due to the majority voting rule, currently the
SGB ID 15154 when profiled by MetaPhlAn 4 reports the taxonomic label Clostridium phoceensis. This will
be corrected in future database releases of bioBakery 4.”
To ensure consistency with the version of MetaPhlAn and the ChocoPhlAn database used in our profiling,
we will retain the current taxonomic label (Clostridium phoceensis). However, we have clarified in the
Discussion that this species corresponds to Lawsonibacter asaccharolyticus as reported in the recent
study, to avoid confusion and to highlight that both studies identify the same species as being associated
with coffee intake. The revised text reads : “Our observation of a strong association between coffee intake
and Clostridium phoceensis aligns with a recent study that reported a link between coffee consumption
and Lawsonibacter asaccharolyticus. As noted in that work, this species corresponds to SGB15154, which
is currently annotated as Clostridium phoceensis in the version of the database used for our profiling.
These consistent findings further support the robustness of coffee–microbiome relationships across
independent cohorts and profiling pipelines.”
Point 9: The variability within genera (e.g., Blautia, Dorea) is intriguing but raises questions about the
deeper relevance of these associations. Including strain-level profiling and functional pathway analyses
for the identified species could be interesting for further studies to provide more detailed mechanistic
insights.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful suggestion. To explore the potential for deeper
mechanistic insights, we performed additional species-resolved pathway and phylogenetic analyses
focused on Clostridia bacterium UC5_1_1E11and Clostridia sp. SGB14844, which emerged as putative
mediators in the relationship between coffee intake and social jet lag. Using HUMAnN 4.0 and MetaCyc
pathway annotations, we profiled within-species functional variation, but did not identify specific
pathways strongly associated with sleep or dietary traits. We also applied phylogenetic generalized linear
mixed models (PGLMMs) using the Anpan R package to assess whether phylogenetic relatedness could
explain the observed associations, but found no strong phylogenetic signal. These negative results may
16
reflect limited statistical power due to the relatively low prevalence and abundance of these species in the
cohort.
Nonetheless, we agree that incorporating strain-level and functional profiling is a promising direction for
uncovering mechanistic links in microbiome–host interactions. We have now included these exploratory
analyses in the revised manuscript (Results and Methods), with full results reported in Supplementary
Tables 13 and 14.
Method: “Functional and phylogenetic profiling of Clostridia species
To further explore Clostridia bacterium UC5_1_1E11 and Clostridia sp. SGB14844, we performed species-
resolved pathway and phylogenetic analyses. For functional profiling, we used HUMAnN 4.0 to quantify
MetaCyc pathway abundances within each species. A total of 106 pathways were detected across the two
species (48 in SGB14844 and 58 in SGB14895). Associations between CLR-transformed pathway
abundances and phenotypes (coffee intake and social jet lag) were tested using linear models adjusted for
age, sex, BMI, DNA concentration, sequencing batch, post-QC read count, Bristol Stool Scale, and
defecation frequency. Analyses were performed separately per species among individuals with complete
data (n = 630 for SGB14844; n = 77 for SGB14895).
To evaluate whether phylogenetic relatedness among strains could help explain phenotype associations,
we reconstructed strain-level phylogenies using StrainPhlAn with minimum marker detection thresholds
set to 10 across samples. We then fit phylogenetic generalized linear mixed models using the anpan R
package42, modeling phenotypes as a function of covariates and a phylogenetic random effect under a
Brownian motion assumption. Model fit was assessed by comparing the expected log predictive density
(ELPD) of each phylogenetic model to a null model without the phylogenetic term, using Pareto-smoothed
leave-one-out cross-validation. A phylogenetic signal was considered statistically supported if the ELPD
difference (ΔELPD) between the null and phylogenetic model was less than –4 and the 95% confidence
interval (ΔELPD ± 2 standard errors) did not include zero.”
Result: “To further investigate the functional and evolutionary basis of these two Clostridia species, we
conducted exploratory analyses of their metabolic pathways and phylogenetic relationships. Despite their
putative role in mediation, we identified no significant (FDR < 0.05) metabolic pathways or phylogenetic
conservation of these species’ associations with social jet lag or coffee intake (Table S13–14). While their
functional roles remain unclear, these species could influence circadian rhythms through unmeasured
metabolites or indirect mechanisms, warranting deeper functional profiling in targeted studies.”
Discussion: “In particular, two Clostridia species, UC5_1_1E11 and SGB14844, were consistently involved
in the interplay between coffee consumption and social jet lag across multiple predefined mediation
scenarios. Together, the abundance of these two species mediated approximately 10% of the association
between coffee intake and social jet lag. Although the majority of the effect is likely direct, or mediated
through other factors, the observed mediation suggests that these species may play a meaningful
biological role and may represent potential targets for mitigating the impact of coffee intake on social jet
lag. Although these species remain poorly characterized, their membership in class Clostridia, which
includes many species known to influence host metabolism53 and neuroactive compound production54,
points to plausible mechanisms involving microbial metabolites affecting sleep regulation. To further
explore their potential roles, we examined the pathway-level functional profiles and phylogenetic patterns
of these two species. However, we did not identify any specific metabolic pathways or phylogenetic signals
that could explain their associations with coffee intake or sleep-related traits. These null findings may
reflect the relatively low prevalence and abundance of these species in the population, limiting the
statistical power to detect subtle biological effects. Nonetheless, their consistent appearance in
directional models highlights them as intriguing candidates for future mechanistic investigation.”

Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestion. We have added sentences in the
Discussion to highlight the broader public health implications of our findings. The added text now reads:
“Furthermore, we offer insight into the complex interconnection between diet, sleep, and the microbiome,
highlighting potential avenues for public health strategies. For instance, dietary interventions could be a
promising strategy for managing sleep disorders and modulating gut health (e.g., reducing coffee/alcohol
intake to modulate Clostridia species linked to social jet lag). Similarly, microbiome-targeted
interventions, such as probiotics or prebiotics, might mitigate circadian misalignment in shift workers or
individuals with late chronotypes. These approaches could complement existing behavioral therapies for
sleep disorders, though rigorous clinical trials are needed to evaluate efficacy.”
Reviewer #3
I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the
Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate
recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.
Reviewer #4
The authors explored the relationship between sleep characteristics, health factors, and the gut
microbiome using data from a large-scale prospective population cohort, the Lifelines Dutch Microbiome
Project. They performed alpha diversity, beta diversity, and species-level analyses, identifying numerous
significant associations. Notably, they conducted mediation analysis to examine the role of the gut
microbiome in mediating the effects of coffee intake and social jet lag, uncovering novel findings at the
species level. While the research questions are compelling and the use of large-scale microbiome data
impressive, the authors must address the concerns outlined below for me to recommend acceptance of
the manuscript.
Major Comments:
Point 1: The data cannot be found. The authors should disclose the raw sequence data and processed
data, preferably including the database, access numbers, and/or website. Without this information, it is
impossible to verify the discoveries reported in the study. The authors should clearly organize the
processed data for the same 6,941 subjects in the following format:
1. Feature Table: This table should include raw counts, with rows representing features (ASVs) and
columns representing subjects. Row names should be feature IDs, and column names should be
subject IDs.
2. Taxonomic Table: This table should include taxonomic classifications, with rows representing
features and columns corresponding to the seven taxonomic ranks: 'Kingdom,' 'Phylum,' 'Class,'
'Order,' 'Family,' 'Genus,' and 'Species.' Row names should be feature IDs.
3. Metadata: This table should contain variables for phenotypes, disease status, or
environmental/dietary factors. Rows should represent subjects, and columns should represent
variables, with row names as subject IDs and column names as variable names. The authors should
also provide a data dictionary to describe the variables in the metadata in detail.

Point 2: Alpha- and beta-diversity analysis: The authors conducted alpha-diversity and beta-diversity

diversity metrics. As suggested, we conducted additional analyses using Phylogenetic Diversity (PD) for
alpha diversity and weighted UniFrac distances for beta diversity. Both measures showed significant

Diversity (PD), was significantly associated with PSQI score (Shannon: Beta = -0.015, FDR = 0.024; PD: Beta

of the gut microbiome are associated with these sleep characteristics."

Point 3: Statistical Analysis for Repeated Measurements: Since the data come from the prospective
Lifelines Dutch Microbiome Project, there may be repeated measurements for the same subjects. If this
is the case, the metadata should include both subject IDs and measurement IDs. Treating repeated
measurements as independent subjects can artificially inflate the number of discoveries, leading to
numerous spurious findings. The authors should employ appropriate statistical methods, such as mixed-
effects models, to account for repeated measurements in their analysis.
For PERMANOVA, 1,000 permutations is too few; it is recommended to use 100,000 permutations.
Additionally, PERMANOVA does not account for repeated measurements or covariate adjustments; thus,
you can consider mixed-effects model-based methods.
Response:
We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful comment. We would like to clarify that there are no repeated
measurements in our dataset; each participant contributed only one microbiome sample and
corresponding phenotype record. To make this explicit, we have added a sentence in the Statistical
Analysis section , which now reads:
“All analyses were conducted under the assumption of independent observations. Each participant
contributed only one microbiome sample and corresponding phenotype record; no repeated
measurements were included in the dataset.”
Additionally, we have rerun the PERMANOVA analyses with 100,000 permutations, as recommended. The
updated results are now reflected in Supplementary Table S4.
Point 4: Mediation analysis: “Employing the mediation package in R” is not at all sufficient. The authors
need to disclose the method name and reference. The authors need to disclose how the repeated

determined by minimizing the Bayesian Information Criterion through a grid search.”
2. Perform mediation analysis for both alpha- and beta-diversity indices as well.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this helpful comment. In response, we have now revised the Methods section to
provide a more detailed and transparent description of our mediation analysis procedures. Regarding
repeated measurements, we would like to clarify that this study is based on cross-sectional data, and no
repeated measurements were available. All phenotypes and microbiome features were measured at a
single time point. In addition to species-level abundance, we now include alpha diversity (Shannon index
and Phylogenetic Diversity) and beta diversity (the first 20 principal coordinates from weighted UniFrac
distances) as microbial traits in both the univariable and multivariable mediation analyses, as
suggested. These revisions are now reflected in the Methods section, and the updated mediation results
including diversity metrics can be found in Supplementary Tables 8–14.
“Inferring the putative causal relationship linking sleep, gut microbiome, and diet or disease
alterations in sleep patterns influence microbial species abundance and diversity measures, or if
the reverse is true. To investigate this, we incorporated dietary patterns, which we hypothesized to be more
likely to be an exposure than a consequence to the microbial features, into our mediation network analysis.
This analysis tested three pre-defined potential directional relationships: (i) diet → microbiome → sleep,
where changes in microbial features potentially cause alterations in sleep characteristics, (ii) diet → sleep
→ microbiome, and (iii) sleep → diet → microbiome, where changes in microbial features are outcomes of
lifestyle modifications.
In the first scenario (Figure 4a, Table S10), we observed that most species demonstrated a direct link to
either sleep or diet. However, two species, Clostridia bacterium UC5_1_1E11 and Clostridia unclassified
SGB14844 (both from the unclassified Clostridia genus), acted as putative mediators in the diet-to-sleep
pathway, suggesting a potential mediation of the effect of coffee consumption on social jet lag. Increased
coffee intake was found to boost the abundance of these two species, consequently intensifying the extent
of social jet lag. This interesting dynamic between coffee consumption, the two Clostridia species, and
social jet lag was also observed in the second (Figure 4b, Table S11) and third scenarios (Figure 4c, Table
S12), indicating that fluctuations in social jet lag might impact coffee consumption, or vice versa, thereby
altering the abundance of these two Clostridia species.
Since these two species appeared in a mediation relationship in all three directions, we could quantify the
proportion of mediation based on effect sizes derived from an unpenalized model (Figure 4d). By
aggregating the effects of UC5_1_1E11 and SGB14844, we discovered that the abundance of these species
mediated 10% of the effect of coffee intake on social jet lag. Conversely, social jet lag accounted for only
1.7% of the effect of coffee intake on these species. Notably, coffee intake was found to mediate 59.8% of
the effect of social jet lag on these species. These estimates suggest that variation in the abundance of
these two Clostridia species related to social jet lag may largely reflect differences in coffee consumption.
Along the same line, the connection between many microbial features and sleep characteristics was found
to be potentially mediated by specific dietary factors (direction III) (Figure 4c, Table S12). Similar to the
two Clostridia species, many species abundances could also be affected by changes in coffee
consumption induced by social jet lag. Lachnospiraceae GGB3570_SGB4777, Ruminococcaceae
GGB9623_SGB15076, and Clostridium phoceensis showed an increase following coffee intake, while
Ruminococcaceae GGB9699_SGB15216 exhibited a decrease. Additionally, a preference for a later
chronotype was linked with increased alcohol consumption, which in turn led to a reduced abundance of
Coprococcus eutactus. Poor sleep quality associated with a lower HEI led to an increased abundance of
Flavonifractor plautii. Nevertheless, findings from direction II still revealed that certain species do exhibit
a direct connection with sleep patterns, independent of dietary mediation (Figure 4b, Table S11). For
example, individuals with a late chronotype displayed elevated levels of Lachnospiraceae
GGB3570_SGB4777 and a reduction in Clostridium sp. Marseille P3244 and Clostridium leptum.
To extend the analysis beyond dietary exposures, we also evaluated whether the gut microbiome could
serve as a mediator in associations between sleep characteristics and disease phenotypes, focusing on
gastrointestinal symptoms and mental health conditions (Table S13-14). However, we did not identify any
microbial features or diversity measures that met the criteria for significant mediation in these models.”

Point 6: The statement “To correct for multiple testing, we estimated the FDR by conducting 1,000 rounds
of permutation” is unclear and requires further clarification.
Response: Thank you for pointing this out. To improve clarity, we have moved the description of FDR
estimation to the Statistical Analysis section and expanded it to explain the permutation-based approach
used. The relevant text now reads: “A false discovery rate (FDR) was estimated using a permutation-based
approach. For each analysis, we shuffled the sleep phenotype labels 1,000 times and recalculated
association p-values for each permuted dataset, thereby generating a null distribution of association p-
values under the assumption of no true association. To estimate the FDR for a given p-value threshold, we
calculated the proportion of p-values under the null distribution that were equal to or smaller than the
threshold, divided by the proportion of observed p-values that were equal to or smaller than the same
threshold. Associations were considered statistically significant if their empirical FDR was below 0.05, and
all tests were two-sided.”
Point 7: The authors can also conduct functional (gene content) analyses in addition to the alpha-diversity,
beta-diversity, and species analyses.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. In addition to our taxonomic and diversity-based
analyses, we have now conducted species- level profiling to explore functional variation in two key species
of interest: Clostridia bacterium UC5_1_1E11 and Clostridia sp. SGB14844. These species were identified
as potential mediators in the relationship between coffee intake and social jet lag. Using HUMAnN 4.0 and
MetaCyc pathway annotations, we examined within-species variation in pathway abundance. While this
approach provided a more detailed view of microbial function, we did not observe strong or consistent
functional signatures related to sleep or dietary traits. These results highlight the current challenges in
translating species-level associations into mechanistic insights. The results of the functional profiling are
now included in the revised manuscript and presented in Supplementary Table 15. We have also added a
discussion of the limited functional signals observed, as noted in the Discussion section
Method: “Functional and phylogenetic profiling of Clostridia species
To further explore Clostridia bacterium UC5_1_1E11 and Clostridia sp. SGB14844, we performed species-
resolved pathway and phylogenetic analyses. For functional profiling, we used HUMAnN 4.0 to quantify
MetaCyc pathway abundances within each species. A total of 106 pathways were detected across the two
species (48 in SGB14844 and 58 in SGB14895). Associations between CLR-transformed pathway
abundances and phenotypes (coffee intake and social jet lag) were tested using linear models adjusted for
age, sex, BMI, DNA concentration, sequencing batch, post-QC read count, Bristol Stool Scale, and
defecation frequency. Analyses were performed separately per species among individuals with complete
data (n = 630 for SGB14844; n = 77 for SGB14895).
To evaluate whether phylogenetic relatedness among strains could help explain phenotype associations,
we reconstructed strain-level phylogenies using StrainPhlAn with minimum marker detection thresholds
set to 10 across samples. We then fit phylogenetic generalized linear mixed models using the anpan R
package42, modeling phenotypes as a function of covariates and a phylogenetic random effect under a
Brownian motion assumption. Model fit was assessed by comparing the expected log predictive density
22
(ELPD) of each phylogenetic model to a null model without the phylogenetic term, using Pareto-smoothed
leave-one-out cross-validation. A phylogenetic signal was considered statistically supported if the ELPD
difference (ΔELPD) between the null and phylogenetic model was less than –4 and the 95% confidence
interval (ΔELPD ± 2 standard errors) did not include zero.”
Result: “To further investigate the functional and evolutionary basis of these two Clostridia species, we
conducted exploratory analyses of their metabolic pathways and phylogenetic relationships. Despite their
putative role in mediation, we identified no significant (FDR < 0.05) metabolic pathways or phylogenetic
conservation of these species’ associations with social jet lag or coffee intake (Table S13–14). While their
functional roles remain unclear, these species could influence circadian rhythms through unmeasured
metabolites or indirect mechanisms, warranting deeper functional profiling in targeted studies.”
Discussion: “In particular, two Clostridia species, UC5_1_1E11 and SGB14844, were consistently involved
in the interplay between coffee consumption and social jet lag across multiple predefined mediation
scenarios. Together, the abundance of these two species mediated approximately 10% of the association
between coffee intake and social jet lag. Although the majority of the effect is likely direct, or mediated
through other factors, the observed mediation suggests that these species may play a meaningful
biological role and may represent potential targets for mitigating the impact of coffee intake on social jet
lag. Although these species remain poorly characterized, their membership in class Clostridia, which
includes many species known to influence host metabolism53 and neuroactive compound production54,
points to plausible mechanisms involving microbial metabolites affecting sleep regulation. To further
explore their potential roles, we examined the pathway-level functional profiles and phylogenetic patterns
of these two species. However, we did not identify any specific metabolic pathways or phylogenetic signals
that could explain their associations with coffee intake or sleep-related traits. These null findings may
reflect the relatively low prevalence and abundance of these species in the population, limiting the
statistical power to detect subtle biological effects. Nonetheless, their consistent appearance in
directional models highlights them as intriguing candidates for future mechanistic investigation.”
The Interplay of Sleep Characteristics with Health factors and Gut Microbiome
Reviewer #1:
The authors thoroughly explained their revisions and efforts, and all comments were
addressed satisfactorily.
Reviewer #2:
Thanks to the authors for their efforts in addressing my previous comments. Most
concerns have been largely resolved. However, I have two remaining points regarding
the authors’ responses:
Point 1: This issue relates less to non-normality or outliers, and more to the fundamental
nature of the variables themselves. The authors’ arguments, such as treating them as
continuous and applying transformations, do not sufficiently address the concern that the
observed associations may be artifacts without clear biological relevance. I still believe
that these methodological choices alone cannot rule out the possibility that the findings
lack meaningful interpretation.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s concern that the observed associations might
reflect artifacts arising from the fundamental nature of the sleep variables rather than
biology. As with any observational study, we cannot completely rule this out, and we see
it as a general limitation of the field. However, we would like to address the validity and
biological significance of these variables from several angles.
First, the sleep phenotypes analyzed in our study (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI),
Epworth Sleepiness Scale, social jet lag, and chronotype) are well established and widely
used. Using PSQI as an example, this self-report questionnaire was developed in 1989
(1) and has been widely used to assess sleep quality worldwide. It has been translated
into 56 languages (2) and is cited in 40,788 studies (3). Furthermore, with the widespread
adoption of wearable devices, PSQI scores have been validated against smartwatch-
derived measurements. For instance, Ko et al. assessed sleep quality in patients with
Parkinson’s disease using both PSQI and smartwatch sensors and reported consistent
results (4).
Secondly, in our cohort, we tested the sleep measures against non-microbial phenotypes
and recapitulated well-described patterns. Social jet lag decreased with age (5). Better
diet quality was associated with better PSQI scores (6). Evening chronotype was
associated with higher alcohol intake (7). Each of these findings is consistent with prior
literature and supports the conclusion that our sleep variables behaved as expected in
this dataset. These results are discussed in the Results section (i.e. sleep characteristics
1
are highly associated with diet, disease, socioeconomics, and other factors) and
presented in Table S2. Thus, we believe that these indices do reflect biological facets of
sleep health.
Third, to further support robustness, we conducted a targeted replication of previously
reported sleep–microbiome associations (with results shown in the table below). Most
prior studies used 16S rRNA sequencing and reported associations at the genus or family
level. Because our dataset is species-resolved by shotgun metagenomics, we evaluated
replication at the same genus/family level to match the resolution of the original reports.
For each reported genus- or family-phenotype pair, we applied the same modeling
framework as in our primary analyses and tested whether the corresponding taxon in our
data showed a same-direction association with the same sleep trait. We observed
directional concordance for several taxa (see table below). For example, Bacteroides
showed positive association (β=0.076, p=1.82×10⁻⁴) and Prevotella negative association
(β=−0.134, p=0.027) with PSQI, consistent with earlier reports. Coprococcus was also
negatively associated with sleep disturbance (β=−0.089, p=0.010). Although the total
number of direct replications was modest, this is unsurprising given platform and
reference differences (16S vs shotgun), cohort and phenotype variation, and the fact that
genus-level tests aggregate species with potentially divergent effects, which can dilute or
cancel species-specific signals. Consistent with this, we observed within-genus
heterogeneity in our data (see the Blautia and Dorea examples in the Discussion). Taken
together, the concordance we observe at higher taxonomic ranks supports the biological
plausibility and validity of the sleep measures and associations reported here.

Point 2: The authors appear to have rotated the directionality of exposure, mediator, and
outcome in their mediation analysis, which is not consistent with the assumptions of
classical mediation frameworks. This reorientation also compounds concerns about
multiple comparison adjustments, particularly in the context of an already high-
dimensional analysis. Furthermore, the use of univariate models as a screening step for
multivariable modeling is methodologically problematic. This approach inflates the risk of
Type I errors (false positives) due to multiple comparisons and reduces power to detect
true associations in a joint model (Type II errors). As a result, the final models may be
2
biased—either overestimating the importance of certain predictors or overlooking key
relationships.
Response: Thank you for the thoughtful comment. We appreciate the opportunity to
clarify. We hypothesized that there is a bidirectional effect between the gut microbiome
and sleep and tested this hypothesis using mediation analysis. This hypothesis is
evidence-based (16,17). We did not rotate the roles of exposure, mediator, and outcome
post hoc or based on statistical significance. Roles were fixed a priori, defined by a pre-
specified directed acyclic graph consistent with the hypothesized direction of effect, and
each direction was evaluated as a separate pre-specified model. In human cohort studies,
it is common to define a set of competing directional models, including bidirectional paths,
and to evaluate them transparently. In particular, it is common practice to evaluate both
directions in scenarios where biological feedback is plausible (18,19), and some studies
have even evaluated direction-sensitive serial orders (20,21). Our approach follows this
practice.

Response to Reviewers
The Interplay of Sleep Characteristics with Health factors and Gut Microbiome
Reviewer #1:
The authors thoroughly explained their revisions and efforts, and all comments were
addressed satisfactorily.
Reviewer #2:
Thanks to the authors for their efforts in addressing my previous comments. Most
concerns have been largely resolved. However, I have two remaining points regarding
the authors’ responses:
Point 1: This issue relates less to non-normality or outliers, and more to the fundamental
nature of the variables themselves. The authors’ arguments, such as treating them as
continuous and applying transformations, do not sufficiently address the concern that the
observed associations may be artifacts without clear biological relevance. I still believe
that these methodological choices alone cannot rule out the possibility that the findings
lack meaningful interpretation.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s concern that the observed associations might
reflect artifacts arising from the fundamental nature of the sleep variables rather than
biology. As with any observational study, we cannot completely rule this out, and we see
it as a general limitation of the field. However, we would like to address the validity and
biological significance of these variables from several angles.
First, the sleep phenotypes analyzed in our study (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI),
Epworth Sleepiness Scale, social jet lag, and chronotype) are well established and widely
used. Using PSQI as an example, this self-report questionnaire was developed in 1989
(1) and has been widely used to assess sleep quality worldwide. It has been translated
into 56 languages (2) and is cited in 40,788 studies (3). Furthermore, with the widespread
adoption of wearable devices, PSQI scores have been validated against smartwatch-
derived measurements. For instance, Ko et al. assessed sleep quality in patients with
Parkinson’s disease using both PSQI and smartwatch sensors and reported consistent
results (4).
Secondly, in our cohort, we tested the sleep measures against non-microbial phenotypes
and recapitulated well-described patterns. Social jet lag decreased with age (5). Better
diet quality was associated with better PSQI scores (6). Evening chronotype was
associated with higher alcohol intake (7). Each of these findings is consistent with prior
literature and supports the conclusion that our sleep variables behaved as expected in
this dataset. These results are discussed in the Results section (i.e. sleep characteristics
1
are highly associated with diet, disease, socioeconomics, and other factors) and
presented in Table S2. Thus, we believe that these indices do reflect biological facets of
sleep health.
Third, to further support robustness, we conducted a targeted replication of previously
reported sleep–microbiome associations (with results shown in the table below). Most
prior studies used 16S rRNA sequencing and reported associations at the genus or family
level. Because our dataset is species-resolved by shotgun metagenomics, we evaluated
replication at the same genus/family level to match the resolution of the original reports.
For each reported genus- or family-phenotype pair, we applied the same modeling
framework as in our primary analyses and tested whether the corresponding taxon in our
data showed a same-direction association with the same sleep trait. We observed
directional concordance for several taxa (see table below). For example, Bacteroides
showed positive association (β=0.076, p=1.82×10⁻⁴) and Prevotella negative association
(β=−0.134, p=0.027) with PSQI, consistent with earlier reports. Coprococcus was also
negatively associated with sleep disturbance (β=−0.089, p=0.010). Although the total
number of direct replications was modest, this is unsurprising given platform and
reference differences (16S vs shotgun), cohort and phenotype variation, and the fact that
genus-level tests aggregate species with potentially divergent effects, which can dilute or
cancel species-specific signals. Consistent with this, we observed within-genus
heterogeneity in our data (see the Blautia and Dorea examples in the Discussion). Taken
together, the concordance we observe at higher taxonomic ranks supports the biological
plausibility and validity of the sleep measures and associations reported here.

The feature table includes all post-QC samples (n = 8,355), whereas the analysis cohort
(n = 6,941) is the subset with complete sleep variables and required covariates. To ensure
full reproducibility, we now provide an explicit ID list (analysis_cohort_ids.txt) so
readers can filter the matrices to exactly 6,941 samples.
Finally, the individual-level metadata are owned by the Lifelines biobank. Like any other
researcher, we access these data under GDPR and participant-consent restrictions and
therefore cannot redistribute them. Within these constraints, we maximize transparency
and reproducibility by sharing all allowable feature matrices and derived outputs, and by
providing step-by-step instructions that enable qualified researchers to obtain the
corresponding data directly from Lifelines. For replication of published findings, the
biobank offers a 3 month, no-cost access window, and we are happy to point applicants
to the exact variables and project fields needed to reproduce our results.
The Data Availability section now reads as follows (L697-714):
“The raw metagenomic sequencing data from this study are publicly available in the
European Genome-Phenome Archive under the Dutch Microbiome Project
(EGAS00001005027) and Lifelines-DEEP (EGAD00001001991). The processed
microbiome data generated during this study, including the Feature Table (MetaPhlAn-
derived relative abundances), Taxonomic Table, and Phylogenetic Tree, have been
deposited in Zenodo [doi: 10.5281/zenodo.15292903]. Due to GDPR and Lifelines
biobank regulations, access to privacy-sensitive phenotype data (e.g., clinical and lifestyle
information) requires following controlled-access procedures. Researchers can apply for
access via https://www.lifelines.nl/researcher/how-to-apply/apply-here. Applications are
reviewed for compliance with informed consent, GDPR, and Lifelines' non-commercial
use policies. Upon approval and completion of a Data and Material Transfer Agreement,
data access is provided through the secure Lifelines Workspace or High-Performance
annually for Workspace access (prorated options available). Full dataset access for
replication studies is available free of charge for three months by contacting
research@lifelines.nl. Additional information on data access procedures is available at
https://www.lifelines.nl/researcher/how-to-apply. ”
